segments.text: SERGEY LEVINE: All right.
So like many of you, I like to use
LLMs to help with all sorts of things that I need to get done.
So last night, I came home.
I was pretty tired after work.
And I asked my favorite LLM to help me out a little bit.
I asked it to help me clean the house, fold the laundry,
and make dinner.
Unfortunately, this didn't work, although it
told me all sorts of things that I should do myself.
So what I'd really like is, so that next time, when
you have a request like this, there
is an embodied system, a foundation model sitting
in a robot that can actually do it and not just spit out
a bunch of texts at you about what you
should spend your evenings on.
Now, fortunately, robot foundation models
are quite an active area of research these days.
This is an area that's fairly young
but is growing very rapidly.
Physical Intelligence, the company that I and my colleagues
founded, has been working on this for over two years
at this point.
And there's some nice results.
This is a robot making a coffee, using an espresso
machine for 13 hours straight, assembling boxes in a factory.
Lots of folks are working on this.
There are amazing results coming out
from other companies, from academia,
from many different places.
And when I thought about what to speak about in this talk, I
figured, maybe instead of showing
lots and lots of results, I would zoom in
on a particular technical challenge with these robot
foundation models and some ways that we can start addressing it.
Because underneath all the demos and all the results,
there is a big question--
why is it that with all these really nice results,
we aren't seeing robots that can follow arbitrary prompts
all around us today?
So typically, when somebody does research on robotic foundation
models, they might have a task like this.
Put the corn in the pot.
This is from the bridge data set.
It's a fairly rudimentary kind of research grade
robotic system.
And it's doing the task.
That's nice.
But that's not really what we want.
What we want is something like this, where the robot actually
goes and cleans your house.
And the prompt is not like, pick up these shirts
and put them in the hamper.
The prompt is, I've got guests coming this evening.
Given that line of text, the robot
should understand what it is that you want
and act appropriately, meaning that you
have to complete the prompt that specifies an entire job, not
just an atomic task.
And it's not just about instructions,
you need to make a plan, and you need
to generalize skills to the new context
and really handle this correctly,
including the context when your slides go out
in the middle of the talk.
Oh wow.
It does depend on the people in this room, yes.
So anyway, where was I going with this?
The command is also in context.
So the fact that you've got guests coming,
the way you interpret that depends
on what the robot knows about you, and your home, and all
this other stuff.
So the point is that there is a lot of grounding
and problem-solving that goes into making
this work for real beyond just the one atomic task.
Now, a really powerful tool for this is test time compute.
Hopefully, many of you are familiar with what this does.
In LLM world, test time compute is
how we can solve complex problems
by thinking about them harder, generating more tokens.
It's a way to solve harder problems,
but it also has a less obvious benefit,
which is that it can break down an unfamiliar problem into more
familiar pieces.
So if you tell the robot, I've got guests coming,
maybe the robot has never heard you say that before,
but it can process the text semantically, reason about it,
and break it down into things that it can actually
do, all the way down to like, pick up this T-shirt.
So you can endow robotic foundation models with test time
compute to get them to be better at problem-solving.
We started working on this a number of years ago.
And the key here is that it's not just
about solving a harder problem.
Going from an observation to an action,
the model can break down the task
into bits that are more in distribution
relative to other parts of its training data.
So it can say like, hey, you're asking
me to pick up this object.
I've never done that before.
But what I have done before in my web scale pretraining
is localize objects and images.
So maybe I can localize an object in an image
and use that as a stepping stone,
break down an unfamiliar problem into a more familiar steps.
Here's an example of this in action.
Again, this is a research-grade task.
It's not particularly realistic, but it's
nice for isolating the issue here.
We're asking the robot to make the blue block
the only thing on the plate.
And obviously, there's something sitting on the plate right now.
And you want to react in a way that is correct but also
semantically sensible.
You don't want to pick up the sushi and put it on the table,
because that's a little bit unsanitary.
It's a toy sushi, but maybe the robot doesn't know that.
So the sushi should go into a semantically appropriate
container.
And the reasoning trace here actually
takes care of that and even figures out
that the sushi might be a little unfamiliar to the robot,
so it should actually output a spatial coordinate instead
of directly relying on the action output
to take care of that visual distribution shift.
And then when we run this.
The thinking trace is updated every few seconds,
based on what's going on.
And you can see that this thing does it.
Now, again, not the most sophisticated or impressive
demo, but more to isolate that particular bit of the problem.
And of course, you can optimize these thoughts.
Thinking models are most powerful
when the thoughts are optimized with reinforcement learning.
And here again, reinforcement learning
serves a dual role, which is it curates the task specification
and turns it into something that is more
familiar relative to the robot training data, which means
that you can propose a number of different textual commands
to break up a high level prompt and pick
the one that the robot is most likely to succeed at.
A little example of this here in the top row, the robot
was commanded to put the hammer on the plate.
I don't know why you'd want that, but for some reason,
you do, very unfamiliar out-of-distribution task.
And if you use an off-the-shelf vision language model,
in this case, this is a Gemini, and you ask it to do this task,
Gemini doesn't know what the robot can or can't do,
so it says, yeah, go ahead and put the hammer on the plate.
The robot doesn't know what a hammer is
or how it goes on the plate, and it messes up.
After reinforcement learning, the model actually spoon
feeds the task to the robot, say like, oh, move a little
to the left, so that it's right over the hammer.
And then when you tell it to put it on the plate,
there's really only one option, which is to do it right.
So reinforcement learning helps to bridge that distribution gap.
Now, so far, we've talked about thinking in language,
but that's not the only tool available to us.
If you're cooking a recipe or something like that,
it makes sense to think through the steps in language.
But imagine, you're rock climbing.
You probably don't think like, hey, I'm
going to move my arm 37 centimeters to the left.
It's more natural to think about this spatially,
in terms of locations, in terms of what things
will look like in the future.
And you can have robotic foundation models
that think in other modalities.
Again, this is some older work in a more research context,
but we had some work on following instructions,
where instead of breaking down the instruction into text,
you break down the instruction into an intermediate image.
Essentially, imagine an image of what
things would look like if you make progress towards the task.
That's your thought.
And then condition on that thought,
it's easier to take the correct action.
This works very well, because of course, the image generation
can be pretrained on lots of internet scale data,
associating language with images,
and enabling the robot to imagine substeps.
So to bring this back to large scale robotic foundation models,
the last thing I want to tell you about
is some recent work from physical intelligence
on large scale models that think with
multiple different modalities.
So this is one of the features of the Pi 0.7 model.
It's a large scale vision language action
model that incorporates a lightweight world
model into its decision-making process.
So it reasons about a task in language
and in images, and then grounds all of that down into actions.
So here's a little demo we did here.
Lucy is teaching the robot to use an air fryer.
We intentionally made sure that we
didn't train it to use the air fryer,
so it's an unseen appliance that it has to generalize to.
Out of the box, if you tell it to air fry the sweet potato,
it actually succeeds, although it takes quite a while,
and it fumbles with it quite a bit.
But if you give it a little bit of additional supervision,
it can be much more reliable.
And crucially, the supervision is not in actions.
Lucy is going to talk to the robot in words
and will actually explain the task step by step,
just by coaching it.
And that adds additional data of images with language.
The actions here are not ground truth.
The actions are taken by the robot.
And after this coaching, which is used to fine-tune
the thinking process--
again, there's no ground truth action here,
it's just teaching the robot how to think, essentially.
Now, it can use these multimodal reasoning capabilities
to do the task quite fluently.
So what you're going to see is the text, which is now
generated by the model itself.
And you're also going to see images,
which are intermediate thoughts that the model is generating
to help it do the task.
So here's the language thoughts, and underneath it
is the image thoughts.
And now, the robot can do this sweet potato air fryer
task pretty reliably.
So that's an illustration of how multimodal thinking can actually
make for much more powerful robotic foundation models that
generalize more broadly, even to new appliances
that they haven't seen before.
So some takeaways.
Thinking or reasoning models can allow
robots to generalize better and follow more complex prompts.
And I think, in the long run, that's going to be really
important, because we're going to want these things to follow
much more elaborate prompts than what anybody is doing now--
prompts like, you're a robot butler,
clean the house at 6:00 PM, get dinner ready,
do my laundry on Saturdays.
That's the prompt.
And it might take the robot weeks of operation
to fully do that.
The thinking doesn't have to be in text.
The physical world is complex.
And you should use the right modality for the job.
And I think that there's a lot of really exciting developments
we'll see over the next few years in multimodal thinking.
And we can even use multiple modalities simultaneously
to think at the right level of abstraction,
so that if you're following a recipe to cook,
maybe that's in language, but if you're figuring out
how to use a new appliance, perhaps, you
have to imagine where your hand should go to push the button
or to open the container.
So this would provide both a way to solve harder problems
and more effectively transfer knowledge
from other sources that might be represented
in different modalities.
I'd like to thank both my students
at UC Berkeley and my colleagues at Physical Intelligence, who
carried out most of this work.
And thank you for listening.
[APPLAUSE]
